To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Web server farm population contains a large fraction of sites that could be improved by using CDNs, that the use of cookies and the lack of explicit cache control information are the two major impediments to the use of content delivery optimizations, and that the use of a cache with an implicit expiration time of 1 hour is not adequate for most Web sites.

(1) the Web server farm population has a high percentage of uncacheable and validation-required responses; (2) cookies are widely used and are a major reason for this high percentage of un-cacheable requests; (3) most Web sites do no not use cache-control features of HTTP 1.0 and 1.1 protocols to improve cacheability; (4) the implicit expiration time is strongly constrained by Squid’s maximum allowed values; and (5) a large fraction of the

cookie usage is widespread and indiscriminate, most Web sites do a poor job of using the cache-control features, and the implicit expiration time of client caches is constrained by Squid’s configuration, resulting in sub-optimal performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the properties of Web server farm workload, which is a crucial first step towards the development of content delivery optimization tools.
the design of content delivery systems for the World Wide Web.
the design of Web servers, proxies, and CDNs, which are becoming increasingly important as the Web becomes the dominant Internet application.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of CDNs is beneficial, but not for all sites and not to the same degree.
Web sites should use HTTP/1.1, and should use cookies judiciously.
there is much room for improvement in Web site design, especially with respect to cacheability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of CDNs can significantly improve the performance of most Web sites in the Internet.
the current usage of the HTTP protocol by Web sites and clients does not fully utilize the features of the HTTP protocol, which can lead to suboptimal performance.
the current Web site workload has several characteristics that are different from the client workload.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the current Web workload and usage patterns have changed significantly since the early days of the Web, and the design of future Web systems and applications must be based on a thorough characterization of the current Web workload.
Web site owners should carefully consider the implications of the use of certain technologies on their Web sites’ performance.
the current state of the art for Web content delivery is far from optimal, and the potential for improvement is significant.
